name: Leadership, Confidence and Problem Solving
objectives: Thinking about times you felt proud, name three of your strengths with a real example of each, with each strength backed by something you actually did
Given a wish about confidence or leadership, write a SMART goal with a first step for this week, with all five SMART parts
Before a real conversation or short talk, practice it with AI role-play using Point, Reason, Example, Point, then say it out loud to a person, speaking clearly for about one minute

Given a real problem in a group you belong to, solve the problem in five steps: name it, find the cause, list solutions, pick one and check it, with the problem in one sentence and at least three solutions
For a group meeting, plan and lead a 15-minute meeting with an agenda, roles and action items, ending with who does what by when
When your group disagrees, use listen, repeat, respond and a fair way to decide, keeping it about the problem, not the person, and getting an adult if it becomes unsafe

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Knowing your strengths
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 4 minutes
Goal: Name three of your strengths with a real example of each.
This lesson builds toward: Thinking about times you felt proud, you will name three of your strengths with a real example of each, with each strength backed by something you actually did.
Confidence grows when you know what you are good at. Strengths are not only grades or sports. Being a good listener, staying calm, making people laugh, being organized or never giving up are strengths too.
Think of times you felt proud or people thanked you. What did you do? That points to a strength. You can also ask people who know you: a coach, a teacher, a friend or a family member.
AI can help you find words for your strengths. Tell it a story (no private details) and ask: "What strengths does this show?" You decide which ones fit.
Step by step:
- Remember two or three times you felt proud.
- Write what you did in each one.
- Ask a trusted person or AI what strengths that shows.
- Pick three and write one example for each.
Words to know:
- Strength: something you do well or a quality that helps you and others.
- Confidence: trusting that you can handle something.
Try it now: Write about one time you felt proud, in three sentences. Ask an AI assistant or a trusted person what strengths it shows. Write down your top three strengths with one example each.
You can now name three of your strengths and back each one with an example.

check.q: Which of these counts as a strength?
options: Staying calm when things go wrong
check.why: Strengths include qualities like staying calm, listening and being organized, not only grades or sports.

check.q: You are not sure what your strengths are. What is a good next step?
options: Ask a coach, teacher or friend what they see in you
check.why: People who know you can help you see strengths you miss.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Setting a goal you can reach
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Turn a wish into a SMART goal with a first step.
This lesson builds toward: Given a wish about confidence or leadership, you will write a SMART goal with a first step for this week, with all five SMART parts.
"I want to be better at public speaking" is a wish. "I will speak once in every class discussion for the next two weeks" is a goal. Goals that work are SMART: specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound.
AI can help: "Turn this into a SMART goal: I want to be more confident in my soccer team." Then make it yours by checking it is realistic for your life.
Every goal needs a first step you can do this week. Small wins build confidence.
Step by step:
- Write your wish.
- Make it specific and measurable.
- Check it is realistic and matters to you.
- Add a deadline and a first step for this week.
Words to know:
- SMART goal: a goal that is specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound.
Try it now: Write one wish about confidence or leadership. Turn it into a SMART goal (with AI's help if you want), then write the first step you will take this week.
You can now set a SMART goal with a first step.

check.q: What does the M in SMART stand for?
check.why: SMART stands for specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound.

check.q: Your goal is "Lead a meeting every week for a year" but you have little free time. What do you change?
options: Make it achievable, like leading one meeting this month
check.why: A goal must be realistic for your life; small wins build confidence.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Practicing speaking up with AI role-play
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Practice a hard conversation or short speech with AI before doing it for real.
This lesson builds toward: Before a real conversation or short talk, you will practice it with AI role-play using Point, Reason, Example, Point, then say it out loud to a person, speaking clearly for about one minute.
Speaking up gets easier with practice. AI can play a role so you can practice: "Pretend you are my club adviser. I want to ask to start a new project. Ask me tough questions."
Practice the PREP pattern for short talks: Point (say your main idea), Reason (why), Example (a real one), Point again. It keeps you clear even when you are nervous.
After practicing with AI, practice out loud with a friend or family member. Real people react in ways AI cannot. Take a slow breath before you start.
Step by step:
- Choose a real situation: asking a question, pitching an idea, saying no.
- Ask AI to play the other person.
- Use Point, Reason, Example, Point.
- Practice out loud with a real person too.
Words to know:
- Role-play: acting out a situation to practice it.
- PREP: Point, Reason, Example, Point: a simple way to give a short talk.
Try it now: Pick a real conversation you need to have. Ask AI to role-play the other person. Answer using PREP. Then say it out loud once to someone you trust.
You can now practice speaking up with role-play and the PREP pattern.

check.q: In PREP, what do you say first?
check.why: PREP starts with your Point, then the Reason, an Example and the Point again.

check.q: You practiced asking your adviser for a new project with AI. What is the next step?
options: Send the AI's words by text
Practice out loud with a friend or family member
Ask the AI to talk to your adviser
check.why: Real people react in ways AI cannot, so practice with a person too.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Solving a problem in five steps
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Use five steps to solve a real problem in a group.
This lesson builds toward: Given a real problem in a group you belong to, you will solve the problem in five steps: name it, find the cause, list solutions, pick one and check it, with the problem in one sentence and at least three solutions.
Leaders solve problems in an organized way. Five steps work almost anywhere: 1. Name the problem in one sentence. 2. Find the cause. 3. List several solutions. 4. Pick one and try it. 5. Check if it worked.
Example: "Only 4 people come to our art club meetings." Cause: the meetings clash with sports practice. Solutions: move the day, meet at lunch, post the work online. Try one for a month, then check.
AI is great at step 3. Ask: "Give me 8 ideas to fix this problem for a high school club." You and your group still choose and check.
Step by step:
- Name the problem in one sentence.
- Find the cause.
- List several solutions (AI can help).
- Pick one and try it.
- Check if it worked.
Words to know:
- Root cause: the real reason a problem happens.
Try it now: Pick a real problem in a group you belong to. Write it in one sentence, name the cause, ask AI for 8 solutions, and circle the one you would try first.
You can now solve a group problem using five clear steps.

check.q: What is the last of the five problem-solving steps?
check.why: After trying a solution, you check whether it worked.

check.q: Your band keeps missing practice. Before listing solutions, what do you do?
options: Find the cause, like a clash with work schedules
Ask AI to choose for you
check.why: Finding the cause comes before listing solutions.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Running a short team meeting
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Plan and lead a 15-minute meeting with an agenda and roles.
This lesson builds toward: For a group meeting, you will plan and lead a 15-minute meeting with an agenda, roles and action items, ending with who does what by when.
Good meetings are short and clear. An agenda is a list of what you will talk about and how long each part takes. AI can draft one fast: "Make a 15-minute agenda for our club meeting to plan a fundraiser bake sale."
Give everyone a role so the work is shared: a note-taker, a timekeeper, and owners for each task. A leader makes sure everyone gets a chance to talk, especially quieter people.
End every meeting with next steps: who does what by when. Send a short summary afterward.
Step by step:
- Write a goal for the meeting.
- Make a 15-minute agenda with times.
- Give roles: note-taker, timekeeper, task owners.
- Invite quieter people to speak.
- End with who does what by when.
Words to know:
- Agenda: a list of topics for a meeting, with times.
- Action item: a task someone agrees to do by a date.
Try it now: Ask AI to draft a 15-minute agenda for a real or pretend group meeting. Change it to fit your group, add roles, and write three action items with names and dates.
You can now plan and lead a short, useful meeting.

check.q: What does a note-taker do in a meeting?
options: Writes down decisions and next steps
check.why: The note-taker records what was decided so it can be shared afterward.

check.q: Two people do all the talking in your meeting. What do you do as leader?
options: Invite the quieter people to share their ideas
check.why: A leader makes sure everyone gets a chance to talk, especially quieter people.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Handling disagreement calmly
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Use listen-repeat-respond to calm a disagreement and reach a decision.
This lesson builds toward: When your group disagrees, you will use listen, repeat, respond and a fair way to decide, keeping it about the problem, not the person, and getting an adult if it becomes unsafe.
Groups disagree, and that is normal. A good leader keeps it about the problem, not the person.
Try listen, repeat, respond. Listen fully. Repeat what you heard: "So you think the bake sale should be on Friday because more people are around." Then respond with your view and look for what you both want.
If the group cannot agree, use a fair way to decide: a vote, a trial run, or asking your adviser or coach. If a disagreement turns into bullying, threats or someone getting hurt, step back and tell a trusted adult right away. You can also practice tough conversations with AI role-play first.
Step by step:
- Keep it about the problem, not the person.
- Listen fully.
- Repeat what you heard.
- Respond and look for shared goals.
- If stuck, vote or try one option; get an adult if it gets unsafe.
Words to know:
- Compromise: an agreement where each side gives a little.
- Active listening: listening carefully and showing you understood.
Try it now: Final task: plan a small project for a real group: the problem in one sentence, three solutions and your pick, a role for each person, a 15-minute agenda, and a one-minute pitch practiced out loud with AI role-play or a friend.
You can now lead a group through a problem, a meeting and a disagreement with confidence.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Problem named The problem is vague or more than one sentence. The problem is one clear sentence with its cause. Also says how the group will know it is fixed. Solutions and choice Only one solution, or no choice made. Three solutions listed and one picked with a reason. Includes a plan to check if the choice worked. Roles Some people have no role, or one person does everything. Every person has a role, including a note-taker and timekeeper. Roles match people's strengths. Meeting agenda No agenda, or no times. A 15-minute agenda with times that ends with who does what by when. Includes a way to invite quieter people to speak. One-minute pitch The pitch was not practiced out loud. A clear pitch using Point, Reason, Example, Point, practiced out loud. Practiced with both AI role-play and a real person, and improved after. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: In listen, repeat, respond, why do you repeat what you heard?
options: To show the other person they were heard and check you understood
check.why: Repeating shows you listened and makes sure you understood before you respond.

check.q: A disagreement about a fundraiser turns into threats. What do you do?
options: Step back and tell a trusted adult right away
check.why: Bullying, threats or someone getting hurt need a trusted adult right away.
